title: Diversity Deflates Bubbles
text:
Financial bubbles form when prices rise far above the real value of what is being traded. Sheen Levine and colleagues, including the sociologist David Stark, wanted to know whether the ethnic makeup of a market affects how prone it is to such bubbles.

They ran experimental markets in two very different places: Singapore and Kingsville, Texas. Participants with training in business or finance traded simulated stocks for real money. The value of the stocks could be calculated from the information everyone received. Each market was either ethnically homogeneous, made up of traders from the dominant local group, or diverse, including traders from other ethnic groups. During trading, they interacted only through bids and prices on their screens.

In both locations, prices in diverse markets stayed closer to the true value of the assets. In homogeneous markets, traders were more likely to accept inflated prices, bubbles grew larger, and they burst harder.

The authors argued that in homogeneous groups, people tended to trust that others' decisions were sensible and to follow them. In diverse groups, traders were more skeptical of others' choices and relied more on their own analysis, which kept prices more accurate.
lesson: Too much familiarity in a group invites blind trust in each other's judgment. Diverse colleagues keep everyone checking the facts.
people: Sheen Levine, Evan Apfelbaum, Mark Bernard, Valerie Bartelt, Edward Zajac, David Stark
source: Levine, S. S., Apfelbaum, E. P., Bernard, M., Bartelt, V. L., Zajac, E. J., and Stark, D. (2014). Ethnic diversity deflates price bubbles. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 111(52), 18524-18529.
